title: PALMS Design System
summary: Auditing and maintaining the design system and workflow for an enterprise travel platform to reduce misalignment and establish design governance.

story.content:
PALMS is an enterprise travel platform where inconsistent interfaces and gaps between design and implementation were affecting delivery.

My initial brief was to build a design system. Through research, I identified a broader need for design governance. I introduced shared component standards, documentation and a page library, and worked with the scrum master to make design reviews part of the delivery process.

All designers adopted the updated library. No further misalignments between design and implementation were reported during the observed delivery period.

As the business grew, the legacy travel request ticketing system struggled to keep pace with demand. PALMS was introduced to streamline workflows and automate manual tasks, helping back office staff manage the increasing workload. When I joined, the platform had been live for six months and served more than 6,000 monthly active users.

The initial interface prioritised speed to market. A later redesign introduced a more considered visual and interaction language aligned with the brand, but both versions remained live across different pages. Three designers were contributing without a single source of truth, leading to inconsistencies between design files and the live product. My initial brief was to build a design system to bring greater consistency to the platform.

Before building the design system, I spoke with stakeholders and team members to understand the wider context. These conversations revealed that the problems extended beyond visual inconsistency.

This led to The Problem Statement:

**How might we help teams keep design and implementation aligned as PALMS grows, so users experience consistent visuals and interactions across the platform?**

To ensure a thorough approach, I created a detailed plan and reviewed it with stakeholders. This helped clarify why the work was broader than initially expected and secure their approval for the expanded scope. The plan covered the following:

1. **Audit Figma files** Reviewed more than 50 files in the project’s Figma folder, archived those no longer in use, and created an index documenting each active file and the features it contained.
2. **Compare the product and component library** Documented inconsistencies between the live product and the library, identifying unused components and those missing from the shared library.
3. **Rebuild for reuse** Applied atomic design principles to restructure components, replace duplicated variants with manageable properties, and address accessibility requirements.
4. **Document decisions** Created guidance informed by mature public design systems, covering patterns, content and accessibility.
5. **Improve findability** Built a page template library containing the latest approved designs to help designers create prototypes faster.
6. **Agree on a shared design workflow** Worked with other designers to establish shared practices, including checking the library before creating components and communicating updates to shared resources.
7. **Close the delivery loop** Worked with the scrum master to include design reviews in every front end user story. Stories affecting the interface required a designer’s review and approval before completion.

The updated component library achieved 100% adoption across the design team, while formal reviews resulted in zero reported design to build misalignments during the observed delivery period. The shared system gave designers, analysts, engineers, and testers faster access to current guidance and reusable properties improved design efficiency.

**Don’t panic when the iceberg is bigger than expected**

At first, the task seemed straightforward: use an existing design system as a reference and build one for our product. But research revealed that several pain points were connected, and the real problem extended beyond the design system itself. The solution needed to address the wider issues behind it. As the scope grew, I shared the findings and proposed actions with stakeholders. They understood the broader challenge and supported the plan. The work ultimately required 40% more effort than expected, but it led to a more complete and effective outcome.

**Do what you believe is right, and trust your team**

The gap between design and the live product wasn’t unique to our product at Rio Tinto, but we were the first team to address it by embedding design reviews into the development process. Turning that idea into practice took sustained effort from our Scrum Master and Business Analyst, along with the understanding and commitment of stakeholders and the wider team.

approachResults: Reduced the number of active Figma files to 25 and created a Confluence index documenting the contents of each file.
Identified three inconsistent interface elements and added user stories to the backlog to address them. Removed four unused components from component library.
Consolidated four button components into one reusable component and standardised input styles. Reviewed all components against the agreed patterns, rules and accessibility requirements.
Created documentation for components and product patterns, giving everyone on the team access to shared guidance at any time.
Created a page template library with current layouts and reusable starting points to help designers build prototypes faster.
Facilitated a meeting to align designers on a shared workflow and agree on weekly alignment sessions.
Made designer approval a requirement for interface related user stories, embedding design review into the quality assurance process.

title: Solver Action Management
summary: Designing and validating a Kanban workflow for Rio Tinto’s continuous improvement platform.

story.content:
Rio Tinto’s Kaizen improvement process relied on scattered spreadsheets, presentations, and emails, making it difficult for teams to retrieve past learnings and track actions through to completion. I collaborated with a senior designer to bring Kaizen into Solver through a connected workflow for preparation, event delivery, and follow up.

My key contribution was recognising that users already organised spreadsheet tasks like a Kanban board. I translated this behaviour into a proposed action board that made status, ownership, and deadlines visible. Working with design and engineering, I helped prioritise a feasible MVP, deferring drag and drop and an additional table view.

Across four usability sessions, users completed action-board tasks without observed hesitation or errors. The senior designer later confirmed a successful launch after I moved to another project. Although I could not assess post-launch impact directly, testing provided encouraging evidence that the design was easy to understand.

Solver is part of Rio Tinto’s digital problem solving platform within its Safe Production System (SPS). It supports methods such as 5 Whys and Practical Problem Solving (PPS), helping teams investigate operational problems, identify root causes, and track corrective actions.

Kaizen brings cross functional teams together to make practical improvements through a focused event, supported by preparation and follow up. However, the existing process relied on a mix of spreadsheets, presentations, emails, and other tools. Documentation was scattered, past learnings were difficult to find across sites, and teams lacked a consistent way to track action ownership and progress through to completion.

Introducing Kaizen into Solver aimed to give teams a shared place to plan, document, and follow through on improvements. The design challenge was to provide enough structure for clear accountability, approvals, and knowledge sharing while preserving the flexibility of a hands on Kaizen event and avoiding additional administrative work.

The design process began with stakeholder and user interviews to understand how Kaizen events were prepared, delivered, and followed up. The research revealed a fragmented process spread across spreadsheets, presentations, and emails. Past learnings were difficult to retrieve, action ownership was hard to track, and inconsistent documentation and approvals made it difficult to bring Kaizens to completion.

A discovery workshop brought together the product team, business stakeholders, and process experts to prioritise these findings. We aligned on the need for clearer accountability and knowledge sharing, while keeping the process flexible and avoiding additional administrative work.

We mapped the journey across preparation, event, and follow up, clarifying the responsibilities of sponsors, facilitators, leads, and action owners. This informed an MVP centred on a digital charter, supporting files, and action management, with lightweight approval points for the charter and final closure.

The interface concepts explored how teams could capture actions during an event and monitor progress afterwards. To evaluate these workflows, we prepared task based testing scenarios covering action creation, status changes, follow up reviews, and access to assigned work. The planned sessions would help identify friction and guide decisions about which interactions and features to prioritise.

**Research and Discovery:**
Explored the existing Kaizen process with stakeholders and users to understand documentation gaps, governance needs, and action tracking challenges.

**Journey Mapping:**
Mapped preparation, event, and follow up activities to clarify responsibilities, approval points, and handovers across different roles.

**MVP Definition:**
Prioritised the digital charter, supporting documentation, and action management to address core needs without adding unnecessary administration.

**Interface Design:**
Developed workflows and screens using familiar interactions, lightweight approvals, and clear action ownership to support teams throughout the Kaizen process.

**Usability Testing Plan:**
Prepared task based scenarios to evaluate action creation, progress tracking, and access to assigned work, with feedback intended to guide further refinement.

The final design organised Kaizen into three stages, **preparation, event, and follow-up**, bringing the charter, supporting files, and actions into one connected workflow. Users could define the problem, objectives, and responsibilities in a **digital charter**, with approval points supporting progression through the process. A **Kanban-style action board** grouped tasks by status and surfaced assignees, deadlines, and overdue indicators, helping teams track work during the event and carry remaining actions through to completion.

During interviews, I noticed participants using spreadsheet columns as an informal Kanban board when presenting and tracking action items. This suggested that status based columns were already part of their mental model.

Before proposing a new product pattern, I checked feasibility with engineering leads. They confirmed that a Kanban style MVP would not add substantial effort if drag and drop interaction was deferred.

I used this evidence to propose a board organised by action status and due date. The design made ownership and progress visible while keeping the first release technically achievable. When I presented the design to stakeholders, they responded positively and understood the potential additional development effort. In later usability testing, users completed tasks involving the new action board without difficulty.

Usability testing provided an encouraging early indication that the design was easy to understand. Across four sessions, users completed the Kanban action-board tasks without observed hesitation or errors, supporting our decision to build on a familiar way of organising work.

I moved to another project before launch, but the senior designer later shared that the Kaizen implementation had launched successfully. While I could not assess its post-launch impact directly, the testing provided positive evidence for the board’s usability.

This project reinforced the value of empathy and observation as a product designer. Listening to users revealed their challenges, while observing their spreadsheet workflows helped me recognise a familiar pattern we could bring into Solver.

It also taught me to examine my own assumptions. My experience with Notion influenced my preference for offering both table and board views. Discussing the trade-off with the senior designer and technical lead helped me prioritise user value alongside delivery effort and become more comfortable adapting an idea I had invested in.

title: Service Design & Workflow Mapping
summary: A mobile maintenance product that digitises field workflows and connects with enterprise systems.

story.content:
The existing product was an Android mobile based digitalised maintenance paperword application. It allowed field personnel to view digital work orders and attachments and record maintenance information that would traditionally be pure paper based and handled through a central enterprise asset management system. 

Although core maintenance activities had already been digitised, checklist related workflows remained fragmented across paper forms, digital PDF editor and specialised systems.

We conducted 16 interviews across eight business groups. I participated in research planning, contributed to the moderation guide, attended every interview, supported parts of the facilitation, acted as note taker and organised the findings.

The study first explored a broad range of roles, processes and tools, then converged to identify:

- Common pain points across groups
- Requirements specific to specialised workflows
- The strongest customer group for an initial solution
- The business and technical information required before prototyping

Separate journey maps would preserve detail but make comparison difficult. One generic process would be easier to understand but would erase role specific requirements.

I therefore independently created a layered service blueprint combining:

1. A generic end-to-end customer process
2. A customer journey for each business group
3. User roles, goals and behaviours
4. Front-end product interactions
5. Back-end software and system dependencies
6. Handoffs between teams and systems
7. Pain points positioned at the exact process stage where they occurred

Placing pain points inside the process made it possible to connect a visible user problem with its operational or technical cause. Additionally, I validated the system relationships with the Solution Architect to make sure the blueprint aligned with the overall technical architecture.

The blueprint gave design, business and technology a shared view of the Digital Checklist ecosystem. It helped the team compare customer groups, distinguish common and specialised requirements, identify system dependencies and prioritise an initial direction.

The project subsequently progressed into design and development. A later stakeholder review grouped feedback into themes, prioritised issues and translated them into recommendations. I did not participate in that later phase, so it is presented as a project outcome rather than a result directly delivered by me.

I also established the product's design system documentation format and independently authored the available component guidance, covering usage, hierarchy, variants, states, anatomy, dimensions, alignment, content, icons, accessibility, exceptions and product examples.

The blueprint was valuable because it did more than summarise interviews. It organised evidence so that different disciplines could reason about the same service. If I continued into implementation, I would link each prioritised pain point to a product requirement and define success measures before handover.

title: Rapid Discovery & Prototyping
summary: A rapid discovery engagement focused on a complex operational scheduling experience.

story.content:
The planning team relied on spreadsheets, macros and separate scheduling files to manage interconnected long-term and operational plans. Frequent priority changes required manual rescheduling, while data moved through several systems before reaching the reports used by the wider business.

The domain was unfamiliar and technically complex. Before moving into interface design, the design team needed a reliable way to capture terminology, assumptions, users, workflows and decisions.

I proposed a collaborative Product Alignment Canvas as the project's shared source of truth. It remained in use throughout the engagement and helped users, stakeholders and the design team build a common understanding of the problem.

Together with the senior designer, I:

- Joined user and stakeholder meetings and interviews.
- Mapped the daily workflow and the end-to-end user flow.
- Recorded assumptions, terminology, roles and product decisions in the alignment canvas.
- Designed a usability testing approach and incorporated feedback into later iterations.

The senior designer primarily focused on the long-term planning experience. I focused on the short-term workflow: how users would interact with near term schedules, understand generated plans and complete operational tasks.

Using the senior designer's draft flow as the foundation, I applied my Figma expertise to create the interactive draft prototype for 12 user stories.

The prototype helped the team move from abstract requirements to a shared experience that users and stakeholders could evaluate. Three usability sessions were completed with users, and the final design was prepared for engineering handover.

- The Product Alignment Canvas became a persistent source of truth throughout the project.
- Twelve user stories were translated into an integrated interactive experience.
- Three usability sessions with four users informed refinement of the workflow.
- The team completed a clear design handover for implementation.

Working with a senior designer did not mean duplicating the same responsibilities. My contribution was strongest where rapid structuring and execution were needed: proposing the alignment method, owning the short-term experience and turning a draft flow into a coherent prototype that could be tested and handed over.
